"Yet today March 13-14, 1993 seems like a thing for meteorologists to geek out about. And to those of us trapped inside it, the storm felt like Armageddon. For some it was close. And that's just so strange to me. So damn strange."

"I usually feel sheepish about big threads. But the Storm of the Century is worth a memory dump. It requires honesty. My own story inside the storm was dramatic enough to me, but it was nothing compared to what others went through."

"Today my ex lives in the Southwest, in the desert. She doesn't like the snow. Our friends Mike and Eric were very different guys. Mike from Nashville, NC, Eric from Chicago. They're both pastors now. My wife's coworker, a cranky, quiet hero, retired a few years ago."

"This thin & bitter-seeming man, she learned, gave his coat to a student who was freezing. He lost his fingers to frostbite. While I played Vivaldi and Bach over the radio and read storm warnings to no one over the airwaves. Both of us inside the hell of the Storm of the Century."

"Dana learned he'd lost his fingers in a snow storm. In 1993. He'd been a chaperone for students from wherever he taught then. They were on a field trip in the mountains of East Tennessee when the Storm of the Century came. They huddled in cabins as the snow piled high outside."

"19 years later I moved with my second wife Dana  my wife still today  to Worcester; New England's snowiest city. She got a job at a legendary old boarding school. There she had an older coworker who was missing some fingers. He always seemed a little angry. He was very thin."

"We made it two nights in our dark, freezing building. Then power came back for our friends Eric and Mike. They let us sleep on their floor till it came back in our building. My friend Anthony later told me he spent the entire week under three quilts in his West Side apartment."

"I trudged up the hill. A massive pine tree had fallen during the storm and cleaved one end of the apartment building just below ours. Sarah was awake, sitting with our cat and shivering in the living room. Our power would be off for more than a week."

"I was supposed to go home. I was terrified. I got in the shitty Hyundai and drove. It was just over a mile. I made it to the complex, but I couldn't get up the hill to our apartment building. I parked. Later I'd find our engine was brutalized by that mile in the thigh-deep snow."

"Amazingly, the full-time announcer who was supposed to relieve me made it to work on time at 7 am that Sunday morning (March 14th, by then). I can't remember his name now, I only remember he was a violist with the Knoxville Symphony Orchestra. I learned later he lived close by."

"Then I'd play Bach. Or Mahler. Maybe I played Penderecki's Threnody for the Dead of Hiroshima. I don't know. That one would've felt appropriate, though. The world was ending in ice, not fire. That's how it felt."

"So I kept tearing newsflashes off the dot-matrix printer that pulled from the AP newsfeed and reading them to whoever could hear me. I took a call from the TN Highway Patrol. They basically told everyone to stay the fuck off the roads, no matter what. Minus the fuck. I think."

"By 5 am most of the TV stations and other radio stations in Knoxville were down. 80 mph wind gusts had taken out transmitters and shut down power stations. Somehow, for about an hour or so, I was the only voice on Knoxville radio. I had no idea what to do. Not really."

"Lightning flashed and thunder rolled, and across the lake  where my 1st wife Sarah & I lived  the lights flickered. The snow blew harder. It was horizontal. The lights flickered again, and they didn't come back."

"He had a 10-mile drive home. I had faith he'd be fine, but I recall it took him hours. He called me well after my shift's 1 am start time.   Around 3 am I entered one of the offices with an outward-facing window as Vivaldi played over our airwaves. The snow was blowing sideways."
